proof:
# An explicit thin support-triangle exclusion for three actual critical caps

This theorem concerns a specified planar three-fiber critical-cap regime.
It is not a classification of all mixed-depth maximizers and does not
prove arbitrary OC. Its quantitative smallness parameter is the volume
ratio of a body to its three actual supporting halfplanes, not the mass
of one fiber relative to another. The argument uses neither an
unquantified stability modulus nor a limiting assertion about thin bodies.

## 1. Statement

Let A,K,B be full planar convex bodies at integer bases -1,0,1, with
(A+B)/2 contained in K, and no other nonempty integer fibers. Let
y belong to int K and let Q be its genuine raw mixed halfspace depth.
Suppose three ambient halfspaces through (0,y) attain Q. Write their
nonzero continuous normals as u_1,u_2,u_3, and assume these form a
minimal positive rank-two circuit. Suppose each endpoint A cut is
proper and each B capture has zero area.

Put a=|A|,k=|K|,b=|B|,M=a+k+b, and first suppose B is nonheavy:

    b<=a+k.                                         (1)

No global depth-maximizer assumption is imposed. Define

    T={x:u_i.x<=h_B(u_i), i=1,2,3}.

Then T is a bounded support triangle containing B. If

    b/|T| <= 2^(-40),                               (2)

one has

    Q > (2/9)M.                                    (3)

If instead b>a+k, the ordinary centroid in the B fiber supplies an
actual mixed-integer point of depth at least (4/9)b>(2/9)M. In that
case no guarantee for the original source Q is asserted. Thus the
configuration with (2) always supplies an actual point satisfying OC.

No shape condition on K or A is imposed. In particular K need not
be a triangle. The proof uses actual compatibility and genuine ambient
criticality; equal values of three arbitrarily selected caps are not
sufficient.

## 2. Contact, cap profiles, and a quantitative bounded normalization

First each of the zero-area B cuts is its actual supporting line.
For a fixed continuous normal u, write s=u.y and the B threshold as
t_B. The A threshold in the same ambient halfspace is 2s-t_B.
Zero B capture implies t_B>=h_B(u). If t_B>h_B(u), decrease t_B
slightly while keeping the middle threshold s fixed. The B capture
remains zero, whereas the proper A capture strictly decreases.
This contradicts the assumed true depth criticality. Thus t_B=h_B(u).
The original traces are consequently

    A: u_i.x>=2u_i.y-h_B(u_i),
    K: u_i.x>=u_i.y,
    B: u_i.x>=h_B(u_i).                             (4)

Both the A and the K trace families cover the entire plane. For K
this follows directly from the positive dependence of the normals.
For A, choose positive alpha_i with sum alpha_i u_i=0. If p is an
interior point of B, then h_B(u_i)>u_i.p, and hence
sum alpha_i h_B(u_i)>0. The weighted sum of the A thresholds in
(4) is strictly negative. A point strictly outside all three A
captures would contradict that weighted sum.

Let u<=v<=w be the three captured A areas. The ordinary positive-part
cover lemma states that a planar body L covered by caps of areas c_i
satisfies

    |L|<=sum_i(c_i-alpha)_+ +(9/4)alpha

for every alpha>=0. It follows by sequentially trimming deeper
parallel caps until all retained cap areas are at most alpha, then
applying ordinary Grünbaum to the retained body's centroid. A complete
proof is Section 3 of
`candidate cce182d75ffe5c52`.
Apply it with alpha=u on A and alpha=Q-w on K. With
F=u+v+w/4 this gives

    a<=w+v+u/4,
    k<=(9/4)Q-F,
    a+k<=(9/4)Q+(3/4)(w-u).                        (5)

Genuine criticality also gives w<=2Q/3. Keep the continuous normal
and middle threshold of that cap fixed, and vary its integer
coefficient until the endpoint captured areas agree at t,t.
Continuity supplies such a coefficient. For t>0, actual midpoint
containment and ordinary Brunn--Minkowski bound the unchanged middle
cap q=Q-w below by t; for t=0 the same inequality is trivial.
Criticality gives w<=2t. Thus w<=2q, as claimed. Consequently

    a+k<=11Q/4.                                    (6)

Assume for contradiction Q<=2M/9. From (6) one obtains

    (9/2)Q<=M<=b+(11/4)Q,
    Q<=4b/7,
    k<=9b/7,                                       (7)

where the last inequality uses the middle profile k<=(9/4)Q-F and
F>=0. The ordinary comparison Q>=(4/9)k also follows automatically
because the middle traces cover K and each has volume at most Q.

We now normalize only the continuous coordinates, identically on all
three fibers. Choose a maximum-area inscribed triangle of B, whose
existence follows from compactness of B^3 and continuity of triangle
area. Its positive area allows an invertible affine map sending its
vertices to (0,0),(1,0),(0,1). Replacing any one of those vertices by
any point of B shows that every barycentric coordinate of that point
has absolute value at most one. In particular the normalized B lies
in [-1,1]^2 and has area between 1/2 and 4.

Translate by the centroid (1/3,1/3) of this inscribed triangle. The
triangle contains the Euclidean ball of radius 1/(3sqrt(2)), while
the shifted square lies in the ball of radius 4sqrt(2)/3. We retain
the convenient weaker bounds

    (1/5)B_2 subset B subset 2B_2,
    1/2<=b<=4.                                    (8)

All areas scale by the same positive determinant. Ratios, compatibility,
the nonheavy condition, and (2) are preserved; the integer coordinate is
unchanged. Continue using the same names for the transformed objects.
Normalize each u_i to Euclidean length one and write h_i=h_B(u_i),
so 1/5<=h_i<=2. The source y need not be zero in this normalization.

There is a useful uniform radius around y. Fix p in A. Compatibility
and (8) put the ball of radius 1/10 centered at p/2 inside K. For
any x in K, the triangle with vertex x and the perpendicular diameter
of that ball has area (1/10)|x-p/2| and lies in K. Therefore

    |x-p/2|<=10k.

Applying this to x=y, and then to arbitrary x, proves

    K-y subset R B_2,
    2y-A subset R B_2,
    R=20k<=180b/7.                                 (9)

The second inclusion uses the same estimate with each p in A. No
bound on a fiber's diameter is inferred from its area alone; the
actual midpoint ball in K is what supplies (9).

## 3. A large support triangle forces nearly opposite normals

List the unit normals cyclically and let their successive angular
gaps be theta_1,theta_2,theta_3. Since T is a bounded triangle and
0 is interior to B, each gap is in (0,pi) and their sum is 2pi.
Put max theta_i=pi-tau, so 0<tau<=pi/3. Each of the other gaps is
at least 2tau: subtracting the other two upper bounds pi-tau from
their total sum gives that inequality. Hence

    sin theta_i >= sin tau for every i.

Indeed theta_i lies in [2tau,pi-tau], and sin(2tau)>=sin tau for
tau<=pi/3. A vertex of T solves two supporting equations with unit
normals and offsets at most 2. The inverse two-by-two matrix formula,
or its two dual basis vectors, bounds that vertex's norm by

    (h_i+h_j)/|det(u_i,u_j)| <=4/sin tau.

Thus T lies in the disk of radius 4/sin tau. A triangle in a disk
of radius L has area at most 2L^2: choose any side, whose length is
at most 2L, and its opposite altitude, which is at most 2L.
Consequently

    |T|<=32/sin^2 tau,
    sin tau<=sqrt(32/|T|)<=8 sqrt(b/|T|),            (10)

using b>=1/2 in the last inequality.

Choose the two normals adjacent to the largest angular gap. Their
sum has norm

    delta=|u_i+u_j|=2 sin(tau/2)
           <=2 sin tau<=16 sqrt(b/|T|).

Under (2), this gives

    delta<=2^(-16).                                (11)

This elementary estimate is valid whether the limiting thin body
would run from a triangle vertex to its opposite edge or would lie
along a triangle edge. No limiting shape classification is required.

## 4. The two selected caps nearly cover the entire mixed mass

The two selected A captures in fact cover A exactly. To see this,
write c=2y-x for x in A. By (4), membership in the i-th A capture
means u_i.c<=h_i. If x missed both captures, then

    (u_i+u_j).c>h_i+h_j>=2/5.

But (9), (11), and b<=4 give

    |(u_i+u_j).c|<=delta R
      <=2^(-16)(720/7)<2/5,

a contradiction.

For the middle traces write z=x-y. A point missing both satisfies
u_i.z<0 and u_j.z<0. As u_j=-u_i+(u_i+u_j), this forces

    -delta R < u_i.z <0,

using |z|<=R. Thus the missed middle part lies in a strip of width
delta R inside a disk of radius R. Its area is at most

    E=2delta R^2.

By (9), b<=4, and (11),

    E/b <=2delta(180/7)^2 b
          <=(259200/49)delta
          <=259200/(49*65536)
           =2025/25088 <1/9.                       (12)

The two selected mixed caps have actual total area Q each. Their B
captures have zero area; their A captures cover A, and their K
captures miss at most E. Summing their two masses therefore yields

    a+k<=2Q+E,
    M<=b+2Q+E.                                     (13)

Put X=a+k. From (1) and the bad target Q<=2M/9 one has

    Q<=(2/9)(X+b)<=(4/9)X,
    E>=X-2Q>=X/9>=b/9,

contradicting (12). This proves (3).

## Scope and checks

The result is explicit: the sufficient support-triangle ratio is
2^(-40). No claim is made that this constant is optimal. Proper A
cuts are used to force actual B support contacts. The argument does
not assume that thinness alone controls the other bodies; their
bounded radii come from actual compatibility, a contained B ball,
the true source point, and the bad-target volume restriction (7).

The A cap cover in Section 4 is an actual two-set cover, and the
middle error in (12) is a rigorously bounded strip area. Closed
halfspaces are retained throughout; their nonzero continuous normals
make their fiber boundaries area-null. The heavy-fiber alternative
uses the actual ordinary centroid of B; the source guarantee is proved
only in the stated nonheavy case. No integer variable is transformed
or rounded, and no global-maximizer assumption is needed.

This statement differs from the archived nonquantitative
`candidate 1350a6f7ed8eb7d0`:
the small parameter here is b/|T|, and b may be the largest of the
three fiber masses. No ordinary simplex-rigidity or compactness gap
is used.
